newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ economy to expand 3 pct over next 3 yrs - NBNZ.
newsitem.headline: NZ economy to expand 3 pct over next 3 yrs - NBNZ.

text.p: The New Zealand economy is set to expand by around three percent per annum over the next three years, National Bank of New Zealand (NBNZ) said on Wednesday.

NBNZ chief economist Adrian Orr said economic activity was past its trough in the current business cycle, reached through a combination of high interest and exchange rates slowing the economy over the second half of 1996.
The annual growth rate would bottom at two percent, with lower interest rates, increased government spending and rising world growth acting to boost economic activity over 1997.
However, Orr warned in the bank's Economic Forecasts the recovery over the coming year could be an unhappy one.
"Employment growth will be slowing, the unemployment rate rising, inflation declining, the export sector struggling and the current account deficit widening," he said.
Asset price growth, including in housing, was also likely to be subdued.

Inflation was forecast to ease steadily over 1997 and then rise over 1998, although Orr said prompt action by the Reserve Bank of New Zealand would ensure inflation did not threaten the top of the new 0-3 percent target band.
Interest and exchange rates were expected to follow a similar profile, falling then rising, although the swings in interest rates were expected to be limited.
"Even allowing for a deterioration in the external trade position, we expect that the exchange rate will not suffer a significant depreciation over 1997.
"Rather, we anticipate the currency will stabilise and appreciate over coming years at a considerably slower rate than in past years," Orr said.

He said government expenditure would be the dynamo for growth in 1998 and 1999, although it would tend to be short-lived and inflationary. In the face of a higher dollar and interest rates, investment and exports would be sacrificed for increased retail trade and services growth.
Orr said the government accounts were coming under pressure as economic activity slowed.
"Having peaked at 3.2 percent of GDP (Gross Domestic Product) in June 1996, the operating surplus is expected to be under 2.5 percent of GDP over the next three years."

The NBNZ said once additional spending and slower growth were factored in, the NZ$5 billion extra spending the government has committed to over the next three years would end up closer to $6.5 billion.
